The Science of Baking: Ratios, Ingredients and Heat

Professional bakers do not follow recipes blindly: they understand what each ingredient does and they work in weights and ratios. This module teaches baker's percentages, gluten control, the jobs of fat, eggs and sugar, how to choose and measure leaveners, and how to make an ordinary home or gas oven bake predictably.
Flour, gluten and baker's percentages
Choose the right flour for bread, cakes and pastry by its protein content
Control how much gluten develops by changing water, mixing and fat

Wheat flour contains two proteins, **glutenin** and **gliadin**. On their own they do nothing. When you add water and then mix or knead, they link together into a stretchy, elastic network called **gluten**. Gluten traps gas, so it is the skeleton of bread. In cakes and pastry, too much gluten makes the result tough, chewy or shrunken. Every advanced baker therefore asks one question first: how much gluten do I want in this product?

Four levers that control gluten
**Water:** gluten cannot form without it. Less water (as in shortcrust) means less gluten.
**Mixing time:** kneading builds gluten; for cakes you mix flour only until it disappears.
**Fat:** fat coats flour proteins and blocks them from joining. This is literally where the word shortening comes from: fat shortens gluten strands.
**Sugar and acid:** sugar holds on to water, so less is available for gluten; acids such as buttermilk also tenderise.

Baker's percentages: the professional language

In a bakery, recipes are called **formulas** and are written in baker's percentages. The total flour weight is always 100%. Every other ingredient is shown as a percentage of the flour, not of the whole dough. So a bread dough with 65% water uses 65 g of water for every 100 g of flour. This makes it very easy to compare recipes, spot a mistake, and scale up for a big order.
Weigh every ingredient in grams (cups and spoons vary too much for professional work).
Divide each ingredient's weight by the flour weight.
Multiply by 100 to get the percentage.
To scale, multiply the new flour weight by each percentage and divide by 100.
Worked example: converting and scaling a soft roll formula
For example, Ngozi bakes dinner rolls in Enugu. Her test batch uses 500 g flour, 300 g water, 10 g salt, 5 g instant yeast, 40 g sugar and 30 g butter. A caterer orders a batch three times bigger.
Water: 300 divided by 500 = 0.60, so 60%.
New flour weight for three batches: 500 x 3 = 1,500 g.
Water: 1,500 x 60 / 100 = 900 g. Salt: 1,500 x 2% = 30 g. Yeast: 15 g. Sugar: 120 g. Butter: 90 g.
Check the total dough: 1,500 + 900 + 30 + 15 + 120 + 90 = 2,655 g. If each roll is 60 g, that is 2,655 / 60 = 44 rolls, with 15 g left over.
Ngozi's formula is 100% flour, 60% water, 2% salt, 1% yeast, 8% sugar, 6% butter. She can now scale to any order size in under a minute and know exactly how many rolls she will get.

Notice that salt at around 2% and instant yeast at around 1% are normal for bread. If a formula you find online shows 6% salt, you will now spot the error before you waste a bag of flour. Hydration, the water percentage, also tells you how the dough will feel: about 55 to 60% is firm and easy to shape, 65 to 70% is soft and slightly sticky, and above 75% is a wet dough that needs special handling.
Weigh, do not scoop
One cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 g to 150 g depending on how it is scooped. A digital kitchen scale that reads in 1 g steps is the single most important tool for this course.

Butter is not pure fat. It is roughly 80% fat with most of the rest water, and that water turns to steam in the oven, which helps puff pastry rise. Oil is 100% fat and stays liquid when cool, which is why oil cakes feel moister the next day than butter cakes, even though butter tastes richer.
Heat is the enemy of creaming

In a hot Nigerian kitchen butter can turn greasy before you finish mixing. If the butter looks shiny and oily, it can no longer hold air. Chill it for 10 minutes, mix in the coolest part of the day, and stand the bowl in a tray of cool water if needed.
Eggs: builders, binders and emulsifiers

A large egg without its shell weighs about 50 g, and roughly three quarters of that is water. **Egg whites** are mostly water and protein. When whisked they trap air, and in the oven the proteins set, so they hold up sponges and meringues. **Yolks** contain fat and **lecithin**, a natural emulsifier that helps water and fat stay mixed. That is why a curdled cake batter often comes back together when you add a little flour, and why yolks make custards smooth.
Too few eggs: weak structure, the cake sinks or crumbles.
Too many eggs: rubbery, dry, eggy smell.
Cold eggs added to creamed butter: the fat hardens and the batter curdles. Use eggs at room temperature.
Sugar does much more than sweeten
**Tenderises:** it holds water, leaving less for gluten, and delays egg proteins from setting.
**Aerates:** sharp sugar crystals cut air pockets into butter during creaming.
**Keeps cakes moist:** sugar attracts moisture, so it slows staling.
**Browns:** sugar caramelises and takes part in the Maillard reaction, giving colour and flavour.
**Feeds yeast:** a little sugar speeds fermentation; a lot (above about 10% of flour) slows it.

Worked example: cutting sugar without ruining a cake
For example, Halima in Kaduna has a customer who wants a less sweet vanilla butter cake. Her formula is 250 g flour, 250 g sugar, 250 g butter, 250 g egg (about 5 eggs) and 125 g milk.
She cuts sugar by 20%: 250 x 0.8 = 200 g. That removes 50 g of a tenderiser.
Because sugar also kept the cake moist, she adds 25 g more milk (125 + 25 = 150 g) to replace some lost moisture.
Less sugar means less browning, so she checks the cake 3 to 5 minutes earlier and relies on the skewer test, not colour.
She notes that with less sugar the cake will stale faster, so she tells the customer to eat it within two days or refrigerate it.
The cake is noticeably less sweet but still tender and moist. Halima records the new version as a separate formula: 100% flour, 80% sugar, 100% butter, 100% egg, 60% milk.
Big cuts, beyond about a quarter of the sugar, usually change the texture too much. For a truly low-sugar product it is better to choose a recipe designed for it than to keep cutting a classic one.
Swapping ingredients safely
**Butter to oil:** use about 80 g of oil for every 100 g of butter (butter is about 80% fat), and switch to a method that does not rely on creaming, because oil cannot hold air.
**Granulated sugar to brown sugar:** brown sugar carries molasses, which is acidic and moist; expect a softer, darker, slightly denser cake.
**Whole eggs to extra yolks:** a richer, more tender, more yellow crumb, but less lift and structure.
**Milk to water:** paler crust, because milk sugars and proteins help browning, and a slightly less tender crumb.

Leavening: air, steam, baking powder, soda and yeast
Name the three ways baked goods rise: air, steam and carbon dioxide

Nothing rises unless gas expands inside it. There are only three sources of that gas: **air** you beat in, **steam** made from water in the oven, and **carbon dioxide** made by chemical leaveners or yeast. Almost every product uses more than one. A Victoria sponge uses creamed-in air plus baking powder. Choux pastry uses only steam. Bread uses carbon dioxide from yeast, plus steam in the first minutes of baking.

A good dome on a cupcake comes from air, steam and carbon dioxide working together.

Baking soda and baking powder

**Baking soda** is sodium bicarbonate. It needs an acid to release carbon dioxide: buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon juice, brown sugar, natural cocoa or honey. Without enough acid, leftover soda tastes soapy and metallic and turns the crumb yellowish. Soda reacts as soon as it is wet, so batters made with soda only should go into the oven quickly.

**Baking powder** is soda already mixed with dry acid salts and a little starch to keep it dry. Most baking powder sold today is **double acting**: some gas is released when it gets wet, and more when it gets hot in the oven. That makes it forgiving if your batter waits a few minutes while you fill several tins.

Freshness test

Baking powder: stir half a teaspoon into a little hot water; it should fizz strongly. Baking soda: add a few drops of vinegar or lemon juice; it should bubble at once. Store both tightly closed, because humid air slowly uses them up.
More is not better

Too much chemical leavener makes bubbles grow so big that they join, rise to the top and burst. The cake rises fast, then sinks in the middle, with a coarse crumb and a bitter or salty taste. Too little gives a dense, heavy, tight crumb. If a formula seems wrong, compare it with the guide amounts above.
Worked example: checking the leavener in a buttermilk cake
For example, Bisi in Ibadan found a red velvet recipe online for a 750 g flour batch. It lists 6 tsp baking powder and 3 tsp baking soda, and her trial cakes sank and tasted bitter.
Guide for baking powder alone: 750 / 125 = 6 portions, so about 6 level tsp if powder were the only leavener.
But the recipe also has soda. Guide for soda: about a quarter tsp per 125 g, so 6 x 0.25 = 1.5 tsp.
The recipe has 3 tsp soda, double the guide, plus a full dose of powder. That is far too much total lift and too much soda for the acid in 500 ml buttermilk.
She reduces to 1.5 tsp soda and 3 tsp baking powder, keeping the buttermilk the same.
Second trial: level tops, fine red crumb, no bitter taste.
By checking each leavener against a guide amount, Bisi found the error and fixed it in one trial instead of five.
Steam and yeast in brief

Water turns to steam at 100 C and expands to well over a thousand times its volume. A very hot oven turns water in choux paste and in butter layers into steam fast, so they puff. Yeast is a living fungus that eats sugars and releases carbon dioxide and alcohol; it works slowly and also creates flavour. Module 4 covers yeast in depth.

Steam needs heat fast. That is why choux and puff pastry are baked hot, usually around 200 to 220 C, and why opening the oven door in the first 15 minutes can make them collapse: the burst of cool air stops steam production before the structure has set. For the same reason, a cake batter should not wait long at room temperature in a hot kitchen. Gas starts escaping, and the cake bakes flatter. Fill tins, level them, tap each tin once on the table to release large air pockets, and get them into a fully preheated oven.
Keep leaveners away from children
Baking soda and baking powder look like sugar or salt. Store them in labelled, closed containers on a high shelf, away from children and away from your salt.

Mastering your oven: calibration, heat and doneness
Check your oven's real temperature with an oven thermometer
Map hot spots and position trays for even baking
Adjust temperatures for fan ovens, dark tins and large cakes

The same formula can come out perfect in one oven and burnt in another. Many home and small gas ovens in Nigeria have no accurate thermostat, and some only have a dial marked low, medium and high. A professional does not trust the dial. She measures, makes notes, and adjusts.
A thermometer
A cheap oven thermometer tells you the truth your oven dial may hide.
Step one: calibrate
Buy an oven thermometer (a small metal dial type that stands or hangs on the rack).
Place it in the centre of the middle shelf.
Set the oven to 180 C (or the mark you normally use for cakes) and wait at least 20 minutes.
Read the thermometer without opening the door for long. Note the real temperature.
Repeat at 160 C and 200 C, and write the three results on a card taped near the oven.

If the dial says 180 C but the thermometer reads 200 C, your oven runs 20 degrees hot, and you set the dial to about 160 C to get a true 180 C. Recheck every few months, and always after a repair or a new gas regulator.
Step two: map the hot spots

Almost every oven is hotter in some places. To find them, spread slices of plain white bread across a tray, bake at 180 C for a few minutes, and look at which slices toast first. Darker slices show hot spots, usually at the back or near the flame in gas ovens. Bake on the middle shelf, leave at least 3 to 5 cm of space between tins and the walls so hot air can move, and turn trays front to back about two thirds of the way through baking (never in the first half of a cake's bake, while it is still setting).

Gas oven safety

Light a gas oven exactly as the maker instructs, with the door open. If you smell gas, turn off the gas at the cylinder, do not light anything or switch on lights, open windows and doors, and get the leak checked before using the oven again. Keep a fire blanket or a suitable fire extinguisher in the kitchen, and use thick, dry oven gloves: a damp cloth transfers heat and can burn you.
Step three: judge doneness properly
**Cakes:** a thin skewer in the centre comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs; the top springs back when pressed lightly; the sides begin to pull away from the tin.

**Bread:** a deep, even crust colour and a hollow sound when tapped underneath. A probe thermometer in the centre is more reliable: lean bread is done at roughly 93 to 99 C, enriched bread at roughly 88 to 90 C.
**Pastry:** golden all over including the base. Pale pastry is undercooked and will turn soft.
**Choux:** deep golden and dry; if pale, the shells collapse when they cool.

Creaming: the step most people rush

Beat the soft butter and caster sugar together for about 3 to 5 minutes with an electric mixer, longer by hand. You want the mixture to turn **pale, almost white, and fluffy**, with clearly more volume. This is not just mixing; you are cutting thousands of tiny air pockets into the butter. The baking powder later enlarges these pockets. Too little creaming gives a dense, heavy sponge no matter how fresh your powder is.

Beat the eggs lightly in a jug and add them a little at a time, beating well after each addition. Adding all the egg at once overloads the fat with water, and the mixture **curdles**: it looks grainy and split. If it starts to curdle, beat in one tablespoon of your measured flour. The flour soaks up the excess liquid and helps the emulsion recover.
Folding and baking
Sift the flour over the mixture in two additions.
Fold with a large metal spoon or spatula: cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom, and turn the batter over, rotating the bowl. Stop as soon as no dry flour shows.
Add milk only if needed, until the batter drops off the spoon in about 5 seconds.
Divide evenly between two greased and lined 20 cm tins. Weigh the tins to make sure the layers match.
Bake at 180 C (about 160 C fan) for roughly 20 to 25 minutes, until golden and springy and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack.

Separate eggs and make a stable meringue for a chiffon cake
Fold flour and fat into a foam without losing volume
Choose between creamed, genoise and chiffon sponges for a given order

Creamed cakes get their air from butter. **Whisked sponges** get almost all their lift from eggs beaten into a foam. They are lighter and springier, they slice cleanly into thin layers, and they are the base of many gateaux and celebration cakes. Two classics matter most: the French **genoise**, made with whole eggs, and the **chiffon**, made with separated eggs and oil.
An egg
In whisked sponges the egg foam does the work that butter and baking powder do in creamed cakes.
Genoise: warm eggs to the ribbon
Ingredient (one 20 cm tin)
Whole eggs (about 4 large)
Plain flour (or cake flour), sifted twice
Butter, melted and warm
Whisk eggs and sugar in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, without the bowl touching the water, until just warm to the touch, about 40 to 45 C, and the sugar has dissolved.

Take it off the heat and whisk at high speed for about 8 to 10 minutes until the foam is pale, has roughly tripled in volume and reaches the **ribbon stage**: lifted whisk leaves a ribbon on the surface that holds for a few seconds.
Sift the flour over in three additions, folding gently each time.
Stir a large spoonful of batter into the warm melted butter, then fold that mixture back in. This stops the heavy butter sinking and deflating the foam.
Pour into a lined tin and bake at about 180 C for 20 to 25 minutes, until springy and shrinking slightly from the sides.

Warming the eggs helps the sugar dissolve and lets the proteins stretch further, so the foam is more stable. Genoise has little fat, so it is slightly dry on its own. That is intentional: professionals brush each layer with flavoured sugar syrup, which you will learn in the next lesson.
Chiffon: oil, yolks and meringue

A chiffon cake mixes an oil-and-yolk batter with a separate meringue. The oil keeps it moist and soft even after refrigeration, which is valuable in a hot climate where cream-filled cakes must be chilled. A typical 20 cm tube-tin chiffon uses about 5 eggs separated, 100 g cake flour, 100 g sugar split between the batter and the meringue, 60 ml oil, 75 ml water or milk, a teaspoon of baking powder, and a little cream of tartar or lemon juice to stabilise the whites.
Whisk yolks, part of the sugar, oil and liquid; sift in flour and baking powder and whisk smooth.

In a completely clean, grease-free bowl, whisk whites with cream of tartar until foamy, then add the remaining sugar gradually and whisk to **firm, glossy peaks** that stand up but are not dry or lumpy.
Stir one third of the meringue into the yolk batter to lighten it, then fold in the rest in two additions.
Pour into an **ungreased** tube tin. The batter needs to cling to the sides to climb.
Bake at about 160 to 170 C for 40 to 50 minutes. Turn upside down immediately and cool completely before releasing.
Why chiffon collapses

Grease in the whites (even a speck of yolk), over-whisked dry meringue, greasing the tin, or cooling the right way up all cause a chiffon to shrink and sink. Cooling upside down lets gravity hold the soft structure open until it firms.

Both sponges freeze well. Wrap cooled layers tightly in cling film and then foil, freeze for up to about a month, and thaw in the fridge still wrapped so condensation forms on the wrapping, not the cake.

Build a buttercream dam so soft fillings do not leak
Apply and set a crumb coat ready for a clean final finish

A professional layer cake looks straight, tall and neat from every side, and every slice shows even stripes of cake and filling. That comes from a fixed sequence of steps, each one done before the next. Most problems customers notice, like a leaning cake, crumbs in the icing or filling oozing out, come from skipping one of these steps.
A layered birthday cake
Neat layers and a clean finish start with levelling, syrup, a dam and a crumb coat.

Level and split
Soak with syrup
Dam and fill
Crumb coat and chill
Chilling between stages is what keeps everything straight and crumb free.
Your basic assembly tools
**Cake board:** a thin card circle the same size as the cake, so the cake can be moved and later stacked.
**Cake drum:** a thicker board 5 to 8 cm wider than the cake, for display and delivery.
**Turntable:** lets you spin the cake while scraping; a heavy plate on an upturned bowl is a workable start.
**Bench scraper and offset spatula:** the scraper makes straight sides; the spatula spreads icing and smooths tops.
**Piping bag and round nozzle:** for the buttercream dam, even without decorating skills.
Cool, wrap, chill

Never assemble a warm cake: buttercream melts and layers slide. Cool layers completely on a rack, wrap them in cling film, and chill for at least an hour or overnight. A cold cake has a firmer crumb, makes fewer crumbs when cut and is much easier to stack.
Levelling and splitting
Place the cake on a turntable or an upturned plate on a non-slip mat.
With a long serrated knife held level, cut off the dome using a gentle sawing motion while turning the cake.
To split a layer, mark the halfway height with toothpicks every few centimetres around the side, then cut along the line.
Keep the flat bottom crust of the lowest layer facing down onto the board, and put the last layer cut side down on top, so the top surface is the smooth base of a layer.
Soaking syrup

A simple syrup is equal weights of sugar and water, boiled just until the sugar dissolves, then cooled. You can flavour it with vanilla, citrus zest or coffee. Brush it evenly over each layer with a pastry brush. Genoise needs it; creamed cakes benefit from a lighter touch. Too much syrup makes a soggy, sweet cake that can collapse under its own weight.
Dam, fill, stack

Pipe a ring of stiff buttercream about 1 cm thick around the top edge of each layer. This **dam** holds soft fillings like jam, curd, fresh cream or fruit inside the cake. Spread the filling inside the ring to the same height as the dam, add the next layer, press down gently and check it is level from the side.
The crumb coat

Spread a thin layer of buttercream or ganache over the whole cake, top and sides, and scrape it smooth with a bench scraper. It should be thin enough that you can see the cake through it in places. This seals loose crumbs into a layer that will never be seen. Chill the cake for 20 to 30 minutes until the coat is firm to the touch, then apply the final, thicker coat with clean icing.

Fillings and food safety

Fresh cream, custards, curds, cream cheese icings and fresh fruit fillings are perishable. Keep cakes with these fillings refrigerated, tell the customer to keep them cold, and follow the general food safety rule of not leaving perishable food at room temperature for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is very hot (above about 32 C). Wash hands, tools and boards, and keep raw eggs away from finished cakes.

Buttercreams and ganache that survive the heat
Make American and Swiss meringue buttercream and know when to use each
Heat egg whites to a safe temperature for meringue buttercream
Use ganache ratios for drips, fillings and firm coatings
Plan finishes that hold up in warm, humid weather

The finish is the first thing a customer sees and the part most affected by Nigerian heat. Butter starts to soften at around room temperature and melts not far above it, so a buttercream that is perfect in an air-conditioned room may slide in a hall at 32 C. Knowing several finishes and their ratios lets you choose one that suits the venue, not just the picture the customer sent.
A bar of chocolate
Chocolate and cream make ganache, which sets firmer and handles heat better than most buttercreams.
American buttercream

Beat softened butter until pale, then beat in sifted icing sugar at about **1 part butter to 2 parts icing sugar** by weight, with a pinch of salt, vanilla and a spoon or two of milk to adjust. It is quick, sweet and crusts slightly on the surface. Replacing part of the butter with a good vegetable shortening raises its heat tolerance, though it changes the taste and mouthfeel.
Swiss meringue buttercream (SMBC)
SMBC is silky, less sweet and pipes beautifully. A common ratio is about **1 part egg white, 2 parts sugar and 3 parts butter** by weight, for example 100 g whites, 200 g sugar and 300 g butter.

Whisk whites and sugar in a clean heatproof bowl over simmering water until the sugar dissolves and the mixture reaches **71 C** on a probe thermometer. This is the safe temperature for egg dishes and reduces the risk from bacteria such as Salmonella.
Whisk at high speed until the meringue is thick, glossy and the bowl feels cool, about 10 minutes.
Add soft butter a piece at a time. It may look curdled or soupy midway: keep whisking. Soupy means too warm (chill the bowl 10 minutes); curdled means too cold (warm the bowl sides briefly).
Finish with vanilla and a pinch of salt. Store covered in the fridge and re-whip before use.

Use gel food colours rather than liquid ones: they are concentrated, so they do not thin the icing. Colours deepen as they rest, so mix a shade slightly lighter than the target and leave it covered for an hour before judging. Very dark shades like black or deep red are easier to reach in chocolate buttercream or by starting from a cocoa base. Flavour SMBC by beating in cooled melted chocolate, fruit purees reduced until thick, or finely ground nuts, a little at a time, tasting as you go.

Pastry: Shortcrust, Rough Puff and Choux

Pastry rewards precise temperature control more than any other branch of baking. This module teaches the three pastries every professional must master: tender shortcrust for tarts and pies, flaky rough puff, and steam-raised choux. It ends with a systematic way to diagnose and fix pastry faults.

Shortcrust is called short because the fat shortens the gluten, so the pastry snaps and crumbles instead of stretching. The classic ratio is **2 parts flour to 1 part fat** by weight, plus a pinch of salt and just enough cold water to bind. You already know it from Nigerian meat pie. In this lesson you will push it further into professional open tarts, which need thinner, crisper, perfectly shaped cases.

Method for savoury shortcrust
Cut cold butter into 1 cm cubes and toss them in the flour and salt.
Rub in with your fingertips (or pulse in a food processor) until the mixture looks like fine breadcrumbs with a few pea-sized pieces of fat left. Work quickly so the butter stays cold.
Sprinkle in most of the water and mix with a table knife. Squeeze a handful: if it holds together, stop. Add the last water only if it still crumbles.
Press into a flat disc, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes. This relaxes the gluten and firms the fat.
Rolling and lining without shrinkage

Roll the chilled dough on a lightly floured surface to about 3 mm thick, turning it a quarter turn after every few rolls so it stays round and does not stick. Lift it over the rolling pin, lay it into the tin and **ease it down into the corners** rather than stretching it. Stretched pastry pulls back in the oven. Leave a little overhang, then chill the lined tin for another 20 to 30 minutes before baking.

**Blind baking** means baking the empty case first. Line it with crumpled baking paper and fill with ceramic baking beans, dried beans or uncooked rice, which stop the base puffing and the sides sliding. Bake at about 190 to 200 C for roughly 15 minutes, lift out the paper and beans, then bake another 5 to 10 minutes until the base is dry and lightly golden. For very wet fillings like custard, brush the hot case with beaten egg and return it for 2 minutes. The egg seals any tiny holes.

Flaky pastry works by **lamination**: building many thin, separate layers of dough and fat. In the oven, the water in the dough and butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the fat stops them from sticking back together. Full puff pastry wraps one big block of butter in dough. **Rough puff** is faster: cubes of butter are mixed loosely into the dough and then flattened into streaks by rolling and folding. It rises a little less evenly but is excellent for sausage rolls, turnovers, palmiers and pie lids.

**Letter fold:** fold the bottom third up, then the top third down over it, like folding a letter. Turn the dough a quarter turn so the open edge faces you.

Each cycle multiplies layers; chilling stops the butter melting into the dough.
Why the number of folds matters

Each letter fold stacks the dough in three, so it roughly triples the number of layers. After 1 fold you have about 3 layers, after 2 folds 9, after 3 folds 27, and after 4 folds 81. Classic puff pastry is often given six folds, which in theory gives 729 layers. More folds are not always better: if the layers get too thin, the butter breaks through and the pastry rises less. For rough puff, four folds is the usual target.
The heat problem

Lamination fails when the butter melts into the dough. Then you get a tough, greasy bread-like pastry, not flakes. Work early in the morning or in an air-conditioned space, chill the dough whenever butter starts to look soft or shiny, flour the surface lightly, and brush off excess flour before each fold.
Shaping and baking

Use a very sharp knife or cutter and cut straight down. A blunt knife presses the layers together at the edges and they cannot rise. Do not let egg wash drip over the cut edges for the same reason. Chill shaped pieces for 15 to 20 minutes, then bake in a fully preheated oven at about 200 to 220 C, so steam forms fast. Bake until deep golden; pale puff pastry is often raw and doughy inside.

Choux pastry is unusual: it is cooked twice. First you cook flour in boiling water and butter on the stove to make a thick paste called a **panade**. Then you beat in eggs and bake it. There is no yeast or baking powder. The paste is full of water, which turns to steam in a hot oven and blows each piece up like a balloon, while the egg proteins and starch set around the steam into a hollow, crisp shell. Profiteroles, eclairs, choux buns and croquembouche all come from this one paste.

Heat water, milk, butter, salt and sugar until the butter melts and the liquid comes to a full rolling boil.

Return to medium heat and keep stirring for 1 to 2 minutes, until the paste comes away from the sides and a thin film forms on the bottom of the pan. This dries the paste so it can absorb more egg.

The V test: knowing when to stop adding egg

Eggs vary in size and flours absorb differently, so you never add a fixed amount. Lift the spoon or spatula out of the paste. When it is ready, the paste falls slowly and leaves a **V-shaped flag** hanging from the edge, and a finger drawn through the paste leaves a trench that slowly closes. Too stiff, and the shells crack and stay small. Too runny, and they spread flat. If you add too much egg, you cannot take it out: that is why you add the last portion slowly.
Choux success checks
Film on pan bottom
Paste just warm before eggs
V-shaped flag on spatula
Hot oven, door closed
Deep golden, dry shells
Miss any one of these checks and the shells are likely to be flat, soggy or collapsed.
Piping and baking

Pipe with a 1 cm round or open star nozzle onto a lined tray, holding the bag upright. For profiteroles, pipe rounds about 4 cm across; for eclairs, lines about 10 to 12 cm long. Flatten any peaks with a wet fingertip. Bake at about 200 C for 15 minutes, then reduce to about 180 C for another 15 to 20 minutes **without opening the door**. When they are deep golden and feel light and dry, pierce each underneath with a skewer to release steam and return them to the switched-off oven, door ajar, for 5 to 10 minutes to dry.
Creme patissiere (pastry cream)

Heat 500 ml milk with vanilla. In a bowl whisk 4 egg yolks (about 80 g), 100 g sugar and 40 g cornflour until pale. Pour the hot milk onto the yolks while whisking, return everything to the pan, and whisk over medium heat until it thickens and then **bubbles for a full 1 to 2 minutes**. Boiling is needed to cook the starch and to make the egg safe. Off the heat, whisk in 30 g butter. Pour into a clean shallow dish, press cling film onto the surface to stop a skin forming, cool quickly and refrigerate.
Pastry cream is high risk

Egg and milk custards are an ideal place for bacteria to grow. Cool pastry cream quickly in a shallow container, keep it refrigerated, use it within about 2 days, fill shells as close to serving as possible, and keep filled pastries chilled. Common faults in all pastry

Artisan and Enriched Bread

Good bread is mostly about controlling time and temperature. This module teaches how to manage yeast and fermentation in a hot climate, how to divide, shape, proof and score loaves with confidence, and how to make rich, soft enriched breads such as brioche and a tangzhong milk bread.
Yeast, fermentation and dough temperature
Convert between instant, active dry and fresh yeast
Calculate the water temperature needed to hit a target dough temperature
Use a preferment or the fridge to build flavour and control timing
Judge when bulk fermentation is finished

Baker's yeast is a living single-celled fungus. In dough it feeds on sugars released from flour starch and produces **carbon dioxide**, which inflates the gluten, and **alcohol and acids**, which give bread its flavour. Yeast is very sensitive to temperature. It is slow in the cold, works steadily around 24 to 27 C, races in the heat, and is killed at around 60 C. In a Nigerian kitchen that is often above 30 C, the real skill is slowing yeast down, not speeding it up.
A loaf of bread
Every loaf is a record of how well the yeast was managed during fermentation.

Salt at around 2% of flour weight strengthens gluten and controls yeast, but concentrated salt directly on yeast slows it, so mix salt into the flour rather than onto the yeast. Sugar up to about 5% helps yeast; above about 10% it starts to slow it, which is why rich doughs need more yeast or more time.
Desired dough temperature

Professional bakers aim for a set **desired dough temperature (DDT)**, often 24 to 26 C, at the end of mixing. Then fermentation times become predictable. The only temperature you can easily control is the water, so you calculate it with this simple rule for a straight dough:
Multiply your target dough temperature by 3.
Subtract the room temperature, the flour temperature and the friction factor (the heat added by mixing: roughly a few degrees by hand, more in a machine; measure it once for your mixer).
The answer is the water temperature you need.
Worked example: cool water for a hot kitchen
For example, Efe in Warri wants her dough at 25 C. Her room is 31 C, her flour is 30 C, and her stand mixer adds about 6 C of friction.
Target x 3: 25 x 3 = 75.
Subtract room, flour and friction: 75 - 31 - 30 - 6 = 8.
She needs water at about 8 C, so she uses water from the fridge and checks it with a thermometer.
She measures the dough after mixing: 25.5 C. Close enough.
With a warm dough of 30 C her bulk rise used to finish in about 45 minutes and the bread tasted flat. At 25 C it takes about 90 minutes and the flavour is clearly better.
By controlling water temperature Efe gets consistent timing and better flavour, and she writes her friction factor on her oven card for future batches.

Developing gluten: the windowpane test

Knead or machine-mix until the dough is smooth and elastic. Then pinch off a small piece and stretch it gently between your fingers. If it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, the gluten is well developed. If it tears quickly, mix a few minutes more. Enriched doughs need especially strong development before the butter goes in.
Preferments and cold fermentation

A **preferment** is part of the flour, water and a tiny amount of yeast mixed hours ahead. A **poolish**, for example, is equal weights of flour and water with roughly 0.1% instant yeast, left about 12 to 16 hours at cool room temperature until bubbly and domed. It gives more flavour, better keeping and a more open crumb. You can also **retard** a dough by putting it in the fridge for 8 to 16 hours. Cold slows the yeast but lets flavour develop, and it lets you shape at night and bake fresh at dawn.
When is bulk fermentation done?
The dough has grown clearly, often by around 50 to 100% depending on the formula (use a straight-sided container with a mark).
The surface is domed and smooth with some bubbles at the sides.
It feels airy, wobbly and less sticky when you move the container.
Time is only a guide: the same dough can take twice as long on a cool morning as on a hot afternoon.
Over-fermented dough

If dough smells strongly of alcohol, has collapsed, or feels slack and tears easily, it has over-fermented. The bread will spread, be pale and taste sour. Next time use cooler water, less yeast or a shorter rise. Do not try to fix it by adding more flour.
Yeast works best at about 24 to 27 C and dies around 60 C.

Dividing, shaping, proofing and scoring

Two bakers can use the same dough and get very different loaves. The difference is in the hands: how evenly they divide, how much tension they build when shaping, how well they judge proofing, and how cleanly they score. These are the skills that make bread look professional on a shop shelf.
A scored baguette
Clean, confident scoring lets the loaf open in a controlled way in the oven.
Divide by weight

Always divide with a bench scraper and a scale, never by eye. Cut, do not tear, and use as few pieces per portion as possible. Remember that bread loses weight in the oven as water evaporates. Bake loss is often around 10 to 15% depending on size, shape and bake time, so weigh a few baked loaves from your own oven to know your figure.
Worked example: dividing for a shop order
For example, Musa in Jos supplies a supermarket with 400 g baked tin loaves. His own tests show a bake loss of about 12%.
Dough weight per loaf: 400 / (1 - 0.12) = 400 / 0.88 = about 455 g.
His dough batch is 5,000 g. 5,000 / 455 = 10.99, so 10 full loaves.
10 x 455 = 4,550 g, leaving 450 g, just short of an eleventh loaf.
He adds about 5 g of dough to the batch (5,005 g) next time so that 11 x 455 = 5,005 g, giving eleven loaves with no leftover.
Every loaf now meets the 400 g label weight after baking, and Musa gets an extra loaf per batch from a tiny adjustment.
Pre-shape and rest

Gently round each piece into a loose ball by dragging it towards you on an unfloured part of the table, so the bottom grips and the top tightens. Cover and leave for 15 to 20 minutes. This **bench rest** relaxes the gluten, so the final shaping is easy and the dough does not tear.
Final shapes
**Round (boule):** fold the edges to the centre, flip seam down, then drag and rotate until the surface is tight and smooth.
**Oval (batard):** flatten to a rectangle, fold the top third down and the bottom third up, then roll and seal the seam firmly with the heel of your hand.
**Tin loaf:** shape as a batard the length of the tin, or roll up tightly like a mat, and place seam down in a greased tin.
**Rolls:** cup your hand over a small piece and rotate on the table until a tight ball forms.

If the poke springs back fast it needs more time; if it does not spring back at all it has over-proofed.
The poke test

Flour a fingertip and press about 1 cm into the side of the proofing dough. **Underproofed:** springs back quickly; the loaf will burst open unevenly. **Ready:** springs back slowly and leaves a small dent. **Over-proofed:** stays dented and the dough feels fragile; it may collapse when scored. In a hot room final proof can be fast, so start checking early.

Where you proof matters too. Cover shaped dough with an upturned clean bowl, a lightly oiled sheet of plastic or a large clean bag so the surface does not dry and form a skin. In a hot kitchen, proof away from the cooker and direct sun, and consider moving loaves into the fridge for part of the proof if your oven is still busy with another batch.
Scoring and steam

Scoring is a quick cut in the surface just before baking. It controls where the loaf expands, so it opens neatly instead of bursting at the side. Use a razor blade on a holder (called a lame) or a very sharp small knife. Cut with confidence in one smooth stroke, about 0.5 to 1 cm deep. For an ear on a batard, hold the blade at a low angle, around 30 degrees, rather than straight down.

Steam in the first 10 to 15 minutes keeps the crust soft long enough for the loaf to expand fully, and gives a glossy, crisp crust. In a home oven you can bake inside a preheated heavy lidded pot, removing the lid after about 20 minutes, or place a metal tray on the lowest shelf while the oven heats and pour in a cup of hot water as the bread goes in. Bake lean loaves hot, often around 220 to 240 C.
Steam burns

Steam burns as badly as boiling water. Pour water into the hot tray with a long-handled jug, keep your face and arms back, and wear dry oven gloves. Never use a glass dish for steam; cold water can shatter hot glass. Open the oven door slowly and stand to one side.

But enrichment also makes dough slower and stickier, so the method changes.

Tangzhong: the secret of soft milk bread

**Tangzhong** is a cooked paste of flour and liquid, usually **1 part flour to 5 parts water or milk**, heated while stirring until it thickens to about 65 C. The heat swells the starch so it holds much more water. Added to dough, it gives a very soft, moist, feathery crumb that stays soft for several days. Many bakers use flour equal to about 5 to 10% of the total flour for the tangzhong.
Worked example: a tangzhong milk loaf formula
For example, Folake in Abeokuta wants a soft milk loaf for a cafe. She plans 500 g total flour and uses 5% of it for the tangzhong.
Tangzhong flour: 500 x 5% = 25 g. Liquid at 1 : 5: 25 x 5 = 125 g milk. She cooks them to 65 C and cools the paste.
Remaining flour for the dough: 500 - 25 = 475 g bread flour.
Dough liquids: 175 g milk and 1 egg (50 g). Total liquid including tangzhong = 125 + 175 + 50 = 350 g, which is 70% of 500 g: a soft, slightly sticky dough.
She adds 50 g sugar (10%), 8 g salt (1.6%), 7 g instant yeast (1.4%) and, after the gluten develops, 40 g soft butter (8%).
Total dough: 25 + 125 + 475 + 175 + 50 + 50 + 8 + 7 + 40 = 955 g, enough for two 450 g loaves in small tins with a little spare. Bake at about 175 C for 30 to 35 minutes, to about 88 to 90 C inside.
Folake's loaves stay soft for three days in a bag, a strong selling point for cafe customers who buy on Monday and serve through the week.
Baking and storing enriched bread

Sugar, milk and eggs brown quickly, so enriched breads bake at lower temperatures than lean bread. If the top darkens before the loaf is done inside, cover it loosely with foil. Brush hot loaves with melted butter or a light sugar syrup for a soft, shiny top. Cool completely before bagging, or trapped steam will make the crust wet and encourage mould. Most soft enriched breads without preservatives are best within 2 to 4 days; freezing sliced loaves keeps them longer.
Egg wash and hygiene

Raw egg wash should be made fresh, kept covered in the fridge between uses and thrown away at the end of the day. Use a clean brush, wash it in hot soapy water after use, and never brush egg onto bread that has already been baked.
Additives

Use only food-grade ingredients from known suppliers, and if you choose a bread improver, use a properly labelled, NAFDAC-registered product exactly as directed. Good technique, tangzhong and enrichment can give soft bread without relying on improvers.

Rolled **fondant** (also called sugar paste) is a pliable sugar dough rolled into a sheet and draped over a cake. It gives the smooth, porcelain look customers expect on many wedding and birthday cakes, and it protects the cake underneath. In a humid climate it needs careful handling, but once you understand it, fondant opens the door to the highest-priced cakes.
A wedding chapel
Smooth fondant finishes are standard for many wedding and engagement cakes.
Prepare the base

Fondant shows every bump underneath it, so the cake must be smooth, straight and firm first. Cover it with firm ganache (2 : 1 dark or 3 : 1 white, from Module 2) or a firm buttercream, scraped sharp and chilled until hard. Just before covering, brush the surface very lightly with water or cooled boiled water if using ganache, or let a chilled buttercream lose its chill slightly so the fondant can stick.
How big to roll

The fondant circle must cover the top and both sides, plus a margin. The rule: **diameter of the top + 2 x height + about 5 cm**. Roll to about 4 to 5 mm thick on a surface dusted with cornflour or icing sugar, lifting and turning the sheet often so it does not stick. Thinner sheets tear; thicker sheets sag and crack at the edge.

For example, Ebere in Abakaliki is covering a 20 cm round cake that is 12 cm tall for an engagement.
Rolled diameter: 20 + (2 x 12) + 5 = 49 cm. She marks 49 cm on her worktop with tape as a guide.
She kneads the fondant until warm and pliable, rolls it to 4 to 5 mm, and checks it reaches the tape on every side.
She lifts the sheet over her rolling pin, drapes it over the cake, and smooths the top first with a fondant smoother to push out air.
Working around the cake, she lifts and opens the skirt with one hand and smooths downwards with the other, so no pleats form.

She trims the excess with a sharp knife or pizza wheel, then weighs the trimmings: 1,150 g rolled, 330 g trimmed, so 820 g was used. She writes 820 g against 20 cm x 12 cm in her notes for future quotes.

Modelling paste and decorations

Fondant alone is too soft for standing figures, bows or flower petals. Knead in a gum such as **CMC (also sold as tylose powder)**, usually around 1 level teaspoon per 250 g of fondant; follow the brand's instructions. Leave it wrapped for an hour or so to firm. Modelling paste rolls thinner and dries harder, so bows hold their shape and petals can be thin. Stick pieces together with a little edible glue (a pinch of CMC dissolved in water) and let decorations dry for a day or more before placing them.

Humidity and the fridge

Fondant attracts moisture. In humid weather it can become sticky, and a fondant cake taken from a cold fridge into warm air will **sweat**: water droplets form on the surface. Do not wipe them, which leaves marks. Leave the cake in its closed box at cool room temperature and let the moisture evaporate on its own, ideally with air conditioning or a fan moving air in the room. Store unused fondant tightly wrapped in an airtight container, not in the fridge.
Simple sugar work

Sugar work means shaping cooked sugar or **isomalt** (a sugar substitute that stays clear and resists humidity better) into gems, sails, shards and lace. It is heated far above boiling water, well past 150 C, and it sticks to skin while it burns.
Hot sugar and inedible decorations

Wear heat-resistant gloves for hot sugar, keep children and pets out of the kitchen, use a heavy pan on a stable burner, and keep a bowl of cold water nearby; if sugar touches skin, cool the area under cool running water for at least 20 minutes and seek medical help for serious burns. Never push wires, toothpicks, ribbon or fresh flower stems directly into cake: use a food-safe posy pick, tell the customer which parts are not edible, and use only flowers known to be safe and free from pesticides.

A celebration cake is a design project. The customer brings an occasion, a guest count, a budget and often a photo from social media. Your job is to turn that into a cake that looks right, feeds the right number of people, survives the journey and the heat, and makes you a profit. Good cake designers ask questions first and sketch second.
People celebrating a birthday
Every celebration cake starts with understanding the occasion and the guests.
The consultation checklist

Number of guests to serve, and whether there will be other desserts.
Flavours, fillings and any allergies or dietary needs (for example nuts, eggs, dairy).
Colours, theme, inspiration photos, and any lettering with exact spelling.
Budget range, delivery or pickup, and set-up needs.

Write the answers into a short brief and send it back on WhatsApp for the customer to confirm in writing. Add a simple sketch with tier sizes and heights. When a customer sends a photo of a large cake but a small budget, show them what fits their budget: fewer tiers, a dummy tier, or simpler decoration.
Calculating servings

A widely used celebration serving is a slice about **2.5 cm wide by 5 cm deep**, cut from a tier about 10 cm tall. That footprint is 12.5 square centimetres. To estimate servings, divide the area of the tier top by 12.5. For a round tier, area is 3.14 x radius x radius. Real cutting of round cakes gives a little less than the theory, so take off about 10%.
Worked example: a 150-guest wedding cake
For example, a couple in Benin City wants three round tiers, 25 cm, 20 cm and 15 cm, each 10 cm tall, for 150 guests. The cake designer is Osas.
25 cm tier: radius 12.5; area = 3.14 x 12.5 x 12.5 = about 491 square cm; 491 / 12.5 = about 39 servings.
Total in theory: 39 + 25 + 14 = 78. Allowing 10% cutting loss: about 70 servings.
Shortfall: 150 - 70 = 80 servings. Osas offers a kitchen sheet cake of the same flavour, 30 x 40 cm, cut behind the scenes: 1,200 / 12.5 = 96 in theory, about 86 after allowing for edges.
Total: about 70 + 86 = 156 servings, enough for 150 guests while keeping the display cake the size the couple wanted.
Osas meets the guest count without building an oversized display cake, and the customer understands exactly why the sheet cake is needed.
Engineering stacked tiers

Cake is soft. Without support, a top tier sinks into the one below. Every tier sits on its own **cake board** the same size as the tier. Into each tier that carries weight, push **dowels** (food-safe plastic or wooden rods), commonly 4 to 6 per tier, in a circle a little inside the outline of the tier above. Mark each dowel at the exact height of the cake, pull it out, cut all of them to the same length, and push them back so the upper board rests on the dowels, not on the cake. For transport of tall cakes, many decorators also drive one long sharpened central dowel down through all the boards into the drum.

Weight passes through boards and dowels down to the drum, not through the soft cake.
Delivery and set-up
Chill the finished cake so the coating is firm before moving it.
Use a sturdy box taller than the cake, on a non-slip mat, on a flat surface in the car, with the air conditioning on. Never on a seat or a lap.
Drive slowly over bumps; for very tall cakes, transport tiers separately and stack at the venue.
At the venue, check the table is level and out of direct sun, add final decorations, take photos, and get the client or coordinator to confirm the cake arrived in good condition.

Build in time as well as structure. A three-tier cake is usually baked two to three days before the event, filled and coated the next day, and decorated and stacked the day before delivery, so plan your calendar backwards from the delivery time and do not book two large tiered cakes for the same day until you have help.

A decorated polystyrene dummy tier gives height at lower cost. Tell the customer clearly which tiers are real and which are dummies, and price the decorating work on the dummy, which takes just as long.

Many skilled bakers stay busy but broke because they price by guessing or by copying competitors. A professional price covers every naira spent, pays you fairly for your time, and leaves a profit for growth. Ingredient prices in Nigeria change often, so you need a costing method you can update quickly, not a price list you set once.

**Overheads:** a share of gas or electricity, water, cleaning materials, data for WhatsApp, equipment wear.

**Profit:** a percentage added on top, for savings, new equipment and quiet months.

Use food-grade boxes that are taller and wider than the cake, with a window if possible. Put the cake on a board and a non-slip mat inside the box. Professional bakers do not follow recipes blindly. They work in weights and ratios, and decide how much gluten they want.
They know what each ingredient does, and they make an ordinary oven bake the same way every time.
Baker's percentages
Flour is always 100%
Weigh every ingredient in grams
Divide each weight by the flour weight
Multiply by 100 for the percentage
To scale: new flour x percentage / 100
Normal bread: salt about 2%, instant yeast about 1%
One cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 to 150 grams, depending on how it is scooped. So weigh everything, on a scale that reads in 1 gram steps.
For example, Ngozi in Enugu makes dinner rolls with 500 grams of flour and 300 grams of water. 300 divided by 500 is 0.60.
Times 100 gives 60 percent water. Her full formula is 100 percent flour, 60 water, 2 salt, 1 yeast, 8 sugar and 6 butter.
A caterer orders three times as much. 1,500 grams of flour times 60, divided by 100, is 900 grams of water. The whole dough is 2,655 grams, which makes 44 rolls of 60 grams.
Now if a recipe online shows 6 percent salt, you will spot the error before you waste a bag of flour.
Gluten
Water: less water, less gluten
Mixing: kneading builds it
Fat: coats proteins and shortens
Sugar and acid: tenderise

Flour plus water, mixed, makes gluten, a stretchy network. Bread needs lots. Cakes and pastry need little, or they turn tough. Choose flour by protein: about 12 to 14 percent for bread, 7 to 9 for soft cakes.
Less water, as in shortcrust, means less gluten.
Kneading builds gluten, so for cakes, mix flour only until it disappears.
Fat coats the proteins and blocks them from joining.
And sugar holds on to water, while acids like buttermilk tenderise.
Balance
Builders versus tenderisers
Builders
Eggs, especially whites
Tenderisers
Flour and eggs build structure. Too few eggs, and the cake sinks or crumbles. Too many, and it turns rubbery.
Fat and sugar tenderise. Change one side and you must think about the other.
For example, Halima in Kaduna cut sugar by 20 percent. She added 25 grams more milk for moisture, and checked the cake earlier, because less sugar means less browning.
Leaveners
Check the leavener against a guide
Baking powder: about 1 tsp per 125 g flour
Baking soda: about a quarter tsp
Soda needs an acid in the recipe
Too much: rises, sinks, tastes bitter
All lift comes from air, steam or carbon dioxide. Baking powder carries its own acid. The guide is about 1 level teaspoon per 125 grams of flour.
Baking soda is much stronger. About a quarter teaspoon per 125 grams.
Soda needs an acid such as buttermilk or yoghurt, or it tastes soapy.
For example, Bisi in Ibadan found a red velvet recipe for 750 grams of flour with 3 teaspoons of soda. The guide is 1.5. Her cakes sank and tasted bitter.
She reduced it to 1.5 teaspoons of soda and 3 of baking powder. The next cakes had level tops and no bitter taste. And keep leaveners labelled, on a high shelf, away from children.

A Victoria sponge is equal weights of egg, butter, caster sugar and self-raising flour. Weigh the eggs you have, and match them. For example, Amaka's 7 eggs weighed 378 grams, so she used 378 grams of each.
Cream the butter and sugar for about 3 to 5 minutes with a mixer, until pale, almost white and fluffy. You are cutting tiny air pockets that become your rise. This is the step most people rush.
Add beaten egg gradually. All at once and the mixture curdles.
If it starts to look grainy and split, beat in a tablespoon of your flour to rescue it.
Fold the flour gently, cutting down and turning over, and stop as soon as no dry flour shows. Overmixing makes it tough.
Weigh the batter into each tin so layers match, and bake at 180 degrees for roughly 20 to 25 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean.

Ungreased tube tin
Cool upside down

Whisked sponges rise mainly on egg foam. For genoise, warm the eggs and sugar over simmering water to about 40 to 45 degrees, then whisk for 8 to 10 minutes until a ribbon holds on the surface. It slices into clean thin layers, brushed with syrup.
Chiffon folds an oil and yolk batter into a firm, glossy meringue. Use a grease-free bowl and an ungreased tin, and cool it upside down, or it shrinks and sinks.
Because it uses oil, chiffon stays soft in the fridge, which suits fresh cream cakes.

Assemble in this order
Cool, wrap and chill the layers
Level and split with a serrated knife
Brush each layer with syrup
Pipe a buttercream dam, then fill
Thin crumb coat, chill, final coat
For example, Blessing in Abuja is making a three-layer 20 centimetre cake. Never assemble a warm cake. Chill the layers for at least an hour, or overnight.
Cut off the dome with a long serrated knife while turning the cake, and use toothpicks to mark where to split.
Brush each layer with simple syrup, equal weights of sugar and water. Blessing uses about 45 millilitres per layer. Too much makes a soggy cake.
Pipe a ring of stiff buttercream about 1 centimetre thick around the edge, then spread jam inside it. The dam stops filling oozing out.
Spread a thin crumb coat to seal the crumbs, chill 20 to 30 minutes until firm, then apply the final coat.

Heat whites and sugar to 71 C on a probe thermometer before whipping. It reduces risk from bacteria.

Fresh cream, custards, curds, cream cheese icing and fresh fruit fillings are perishable. Keep those cakes refrigerated, and tell the customer to keep them cold.

Roll a long rectangle and fold it in three, like a letter.
Turn it a quarter turn and repeat. If the butter looks soft or shiny, chill it. Melted butter gives tough, greasy pastry.
Each fold triples the layers: 3, then 9, 27, and 81 after four folds. Cut with a sharp knife, and bake at about 200 to 220 degrees so steam forms fast.
Cook, beat, then the V test
Boil water, milk and butter; add flour
Stir on the heat until a film forms
Cool until just warm
Add egg gradually, to the V test
Bake hot; never open the door early
Bring the water, milk and butter to a full boil. Off the heat, tip in all the flour and beat hard until smooth.
Stir on medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, until a thin film forms on the pan bottom. This dries the paste.
Beat it in a bowl until just warm.
Add egg a little at a time. Eggs vary, so never add a fixed amount. Stop when the paste falls slowly from the spatula and leaves a V-shaped flag. Too much egg, and the shells spread flat.
Bake at about 200 degrees for 15 minutes, then about 180 for 15 to 20 more, without opening the door. Pierce each shell and dry it in the switched-off oven.
Food safety
High-risk fillings
Boil 1 to 2 minutes. Cool fast in a shallow dish, refrigerate, use within about 2 days.
Fill close to serving and keep chilled. Never leave in a warm room or hot car.
Cook until piping hot, not pink. Keep raw meat, boards and knives separate.

Egg and milk custards are ideal places for bacteria to grow. Pastry cream must bubble for a full 1 to 2 minutes. Cool it quickly in a shallow dish, keep it in the fridge, and use it within about 2 days.
Fill choux as close to serving as possible, and keep filled pastries chilled.

Cook meat fillings until the centre is piping hot and no longer pink. Keep raw meat and its boards and knives away from finished food. And anything with a food safety doubt must be thrown away, never sold.
Fixing faults
Find the cause in order
Check temperature and handling
Check oven, shelf and bake time
Keep a batch record. Change one thing at a time.
For example, Rukayat in Ilorin had a tray of custard tarts returned. The bases were pale and wet underneath.
Her batch record showed the usual 200 grams of flour, 100 of butter and 45 millilitres of water. No change.
The dough was rested and chilled as usual.
But she had skipped the egg seal and baked on the bottom shelf, which her oven card says runs cooler. She fixed both, and the next bases were crisp and golden.
Write down weights, room temperature, chilling, oven setting, shelf and time for every batch. Change only one thing at a time when you test a fix.
Key points
Remember
Shortcrust: 2 to 1, cold, ease into tin
Rough puff: four letter folds, keep cold
Choux: dry the paste, use the V test
Chill custard fillings fast; keep cold
Ratio, temperature, handling, baking
To remember. Keep shortcrust cold and ease it into the tin. Give rough puff four letter folds and keep the butter cold. Dry the choux paste and use the V test.
Chill custard fillings fast. And find faults in order: ratio, temperature, handling, then baking.

This is the video for module four of Advanced Baking and Pastry.
Why this matters
In a hot kitchen, slow the yeast down
Yeast works best at 24 to 27 C
It races in the heat, dies at 60 C
Control dough temperature
Shape, proof and score with confidence
Good bread is mostly about controlling time and temperature. Yeast is a living fungus. It works steadily at around 24 to 27 degrees.
It races in the heat, and dies at around 60 degrees. In a Nigerian kitchen above 30 degrees, the real skill is slowing yeast down.
So first you will control your dough temperature.
Then you will shape, proof and score like a professional, and make soft enriched breads.
Dough temperature
Work out your water temperature
Target dough temperature x 3
Subtract room temperature
Subtract flour temperature
Subtract mixer friction
The answer is your water temperature
For example, Efe in Warri wants her dough at 25 degrees. 25 times 3 is 75.
Her room is 31 degrees.
Her flour is 30.
Her stand mixer adds about 6 degrees of friction. So 75 minus 31, minus 30, minus 6, leaves 8.

She needs water at about 8 degrees, straight from the fridge. Her warm 30 degree dough used to rise in 45 minutes and tasted flat. At 25 degrees it takes about 90 minutes, and the flavour is clearly better.
Reading the dough
Judge the dough, not the clock
Windowpane: stretches thin, lets light through
Bulk done: grown, domed, airy, wobbly
Over-fermented: alcohol smell, slack, tears
Divide by weight, allow for bake loss
Knead until the dough is smooth. Stretch a small piece. If light shows through without tearing, the gluten is ready.

Bulk fermentation is done when the dough has grown clearly, the top is domed with bubbles at the sides, and it wobbles when you move the container. The same dough can take twice as long on a cool morning.
If it smells strongly of alcohol and tears easily, it has over-fermented. Next time use cooler water, less yeast or a shorter rise.
Always divide with a scraper and a scale. For example, Musa in Jos sells 400 gram loaves. His oven loses about 12 percent, so he divides at about 455 grams of dough.
Shaping and proofing
Pre-shape, shape, poke, score
Pre-shape a loose ball; rest 15 to 20 min
Final shape with a tight surface
Poke test: slow spring, small dent
Score 0.5 to 1 cm deep, one stroke
Bake with steam for the first minutes
Round each piece loosely and let it rest 15 to 20 minutes, so the gluten relaxes and the dough does not tear.
Shape it with tension, whether a round, an oval, a tin loaf or rolls. Cover it so a skin does not form.
Press a floured fingertip about 1 centimetre in. Springs back fast? Wait. Springs back slowly and leaves a small dent? Ready. Stays dented? Over-proofed. In a hot room, check early.
Score with a razor or very sharp knife, in one confident stroke, so the loaf opens neatly.
Steam in the first 10 to 15 minutes gives a glossy, crisp crust. Bake lean loaves hot, around 220 to 240 degrees.
Safety first
Steam, egg wash and additives
Use a long-handled jug, keep face and arms back, wear dry gloves. Never use a glass dish.
Make it fresh, keep covered in the fridge, throw away at day's end. Wash the brush in hot soapy water.
Known suppliers. Any improver must be labelled, NAFDAC-registered and used exactly as directed.

Steam burns as badly as boiling water. Pour water into the hot tray with a long-handled jug, keep your face and arms back, and wear dry oven gloves. Never use glass, because cold water can shatter it. Open the door slowly and stand to one side.
Make raw egg wash fresh, keep it covered in the fridge, and throw it away at the end of the day.
Use only food-grade ingredients. If you choose a bread improver, it must be NAFDAC-registered and used exactly as directed.
Enriched bread
Soft milk bread with tangzhong
Tangzhong: 1 part flour, 5 parts milk
Cook to 65 C, then cool
Mix dough; add butter after gluten forms
Bake cooler, to 88 to 90 C inside
Enriched doughs add fat, sugar, eggs or milk. They are softer, but slower and stickier. For brioche, add the butter only after the gluten is developed, and keep the dough cool.
Tangzhong is a cooked paste that keeps bread soft for days. For example, Folake in Abeokuta uses 25 grams of flour, which is 5 percent of her 500, with 125 grams of milk.
She cooks it to 65 degrees, stirring until thick, and lets it cool.
Then she mixes the dough and adds 40 grams of soft butter once the gluten has developed.
Sugar, milk and eggs brown fast, so she bakes at about 175 degrees until the centre reads 88 to 90. Her loaves stay soft for three days. Cool them completely before bagging.
Key points
Remember
Water temp = target x 3 minus the rest
Judge bulk rise by the dough
Divide by weight; know your bake loss
Enriched: cooler dough, cooler oven
To remember. Work out your water temperature. Judge the rise by the dough, not the clock. Divide by weight.
Use the poke test before baking. And keep enriched doughs cool and bake them cooler.

Fondant
Cover a cake without pleats
Firm, smooth, chilled base coat
Roll: top + 2 x height + 5 cm
Roll 4 to 5 mm thick
Smooth the top, open the skirt
Trim, then weigh what you used
Fondant shows every bump, so start with a firm ganache or buttercream coat, scraped sharp and chilled hard.
For example, Ebere in Abakaliki is covering a 20 centimetre cake, 12 tall. 20, plus 2 times 12, plus 5, means she rolls a 49 centimetre circle.
Roll to about 4 to 5 millimetres. Thinner tears. Thicker sags and cracks.
Drape it, smooth the top first to push out air, then lift the skirt with one hand and smooth down with the other.
Trim, then weigh the trimmings. Ebere used 820 grams, and wrote that down to cost her next cake exactly.
If a cold fondant cake sweats, do not wipe it. Let it dry in its closed box.
Tiered cakes
Servings and support
Servings: tier area / 12.5
Take off about 10% for round tiers
Each tier on its own board
4 to 6 dowels, cut to the same height

A celebration slice is about 2.5 by 5 centimetres, so 12.5 square centimetres. For example, Osas in Benin City planned three tiers. The 25 centimetre tier is about 491 square centimetres, which is about 39 servings.
All three tiers came to 78 in theory, or about 70 after cutting loss. For 150 guests, she added a kitchen sheet cake of the same flavour, cut behind the scenes.
Cake is soft. Without support, a top tier sinks. So every tier sits on its own board.

Push dowels into each tier that carries weight, mark them at cake height, cut them all the same, and push them back. The weight then passes through the boards to the drum, not the cake. Deliver chilled, boxed, flat, in a cool car.
Worked example
Pricing a 20 cm three-layer cake
For example, Hauwa in Abuja costs a 20 cm three-layer vanilla cake with Swiss meringue buttercream.
Packaging
Overheads share
Labour, 5 hours
Assumed prices. Use your own receipts.

Many skilled bakers stay busy but broke, because they price by guessing. Find the cost per gram of each ingredient: what you paid, divided by the grams in the pack. These prices are assumed, to show the method.
Hauwa's ingredients come to about 12,000 naira. Butter is by far the biggest cost.
Packaging, the board, drum and box, about 3,500.
Her share of gas, power and water, about 2,000.
And her own labour, 5 hours at 1,500 naira an hour, which is 7,500. Total cost: 25,000 naira.

She adds a 30 percent markup, for a price of 32,500 naira. Her profit is 7,500, which is only about 23 percent of the price. So a 10 percent discount would cut her profit by over 40 percent. Offer added value before cutting the price.
Safety first
Sugar, decorations and payments
Wear heat-resistant gloves. Children out. On skin: cool running water 20 minutes.
No wires or stems straight into cake. Use a posy pick and tell the customer.
Confirm money in your own bank app. Screenshots and text alerts can be fake.

Hot sugar goes well past 150 degrees and sticks to skin. Wear heat-resistant gloves and keep children out. If it touches skin, cool it under running water for at least 20 minutes, and get medical help for serious burns.
Never push wires, toothpicks or flower stems straight into cake. Use a food-safe posy pick, and tell the customer what is not edible.
And confirm every payment inside your bank app. Fake alerts are a common scam.
Every order
Label and manage every order
Written brief, confirmed by the customer
Deposit to book the date
Label: storage advice and best-by date
Allergens: wheat, egg, milk, nuts
Weekly production calendar
For every order, send a written brief and get it confirmed. Take a deposit, often 50 to 70 percent.
Label each cake with storage advice, a best-by date and allergens such as wheat, egg, milk and nuts.
And keep a weekly calendar, so you never accept more than your oven and hours allow.
Key points
Remember
Fondant needs a firm, smooth base
Servings: area / 12.5, minus 10%
Boards and dowels under every tier
Cost all five parts, then add profit
Markup on cost is not margin on price
To remember. Give fondant a firm base. Work out servings from the tier area. Support every tier with a board and dowels.
Cost ingredients, packaging, overheads and labour, then add profit. And remember, markup is not the same as margin.
